== Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:531-674

\section{Declarations with Static Parameters}
\seclabel{overloading-static-params}

The rules above compare the parameter types and the return types of
declarations without static parameters.
A declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose parameter
type ranges over every instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their
bounds (\secref{overloading-terms}).
A declaration $d_1$ is more specific than a declaration $d_2$ when $d_2$ is
applicable to every call to which $d_1$ is applicable, and not the other way
round (\secref{resolving-overloading}); where neither has static parameters,
this is the relation $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$ of the rules above.
A set of overloaded declarations, some or all of which have static parameters,
is a valid overloading when every pair $d_1$, $d_2$ of them satisfies the
following three rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each applicable to every
call to which the other is applicable.
\item
The \emph{Meet Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ exclude each other, or one of them is more
specific than the other, or some declaration of the set is more specific than
both and applicable to every call to which both are applicable.
\item
The \emph{Return Type Rule}: if $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$, then for
every argument type other than \TYP{BottomType} to which $d_1$ is applicable,
and for every instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to it, some instance of $d_1$
is applicable to it whose return type is a subtype of the return type of that
instance of $d_2$.
\end{itemize}
\revision{revival-overloading}{The revival's text of 30~September 2026 stated
the No Duplicates Rule as ``$d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each more specific than the
other'', which the strict sense of more specific above made refuse no pair.
It is stated on the relation without ``and not the other way round'', as the
type group's papers of 2011 and 2019 state it, and so it refuses
\EXP{\VAR{dup}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket)}
beside \EXP{\VAR{dup}\llbracket{}U\rrbracket(x\COLON
\TYP{Box}\llbracket{}U\rrbracket)}, each applicable to every call to which the
other is.}
The Subtype Rule, the Incompatibility Rule and the Meet Rule above are these
rules for declarations without static parameters, with the conditions that
coercion adds; the Return Type Rule is the Subtype Rule's condition on return
types, checked over every instance of the less specific declaration and not
over one instance chosen for the pair.

As in \secref{more-specific-rule}, declarations of the set that are each more
specific than both $d_1$ and $d_2$ and that together cover every argument to
which both are applicable also satisfy the Meet Rule.
\revision{revival-meet}{The type group's paper of 2011 states the Meet Rule
without this case.}

Two parameter types with static parameters exclude each other, for the Meet
Rule and the Incompatibility Rule, as the type group's paper of 2011 decides it
by \emph{existential reduction}: each static parameter stands for any type
within its bound, and where the two parameter types, or their elements at one
position, are or extend instances of one parameterized trait, instantiation
exclusion (\secref{trait-types}) lets them meet only where the static arguments
of those instances are the same, every static argument but an operator argument
counting.
So where \TYP{Box} and \TYP{Pair} are distinct object types with static
parameters, the parameter types \EXP{\TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} and
\EXP{\TYP{Pair}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket} of two declarations exclude each
other whatever \VAR{T}, \VAR{A} and \VAR{B} stand for.
\revision{revival-overloading}{The revival's text of 30~September 2026 read
instantiation exclusion here only where the two parameter types mention one
parameterized trait.
The type group's paper of 2011 reads it at every pair of instances of one
parameterized trait among the two types' supertypes, so that
\EXP{\VAR{copyOf}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(a\COLON
\TYP{Frozen}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket)} and
\EXP{\VAR{copyOf}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(a\COLON
\TYP{Thawed}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket)} exclude each other where
\EXP{\TYP{Frozen}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket} and
\EXP{\TYP{Thawed}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket} both extend
\EXP{\TYP{Readable}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket} and exclude each other, a value of
both having one instance of \TYP{Readable}.}

The Return Type Rule refuses the following pair, where trait \TYP{Round}
extends trait \TYP{Shape} and object \TYP{Circle} extends \TYP{Round}:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T = x
%ident(x: Round): Round = x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Round})\COLON \TYP{Round} = x\)
\end{Fortress}
The second declaration is more specific than the first.
For an argument of type \TYP{Circle}, the instance of the first at \TYP{Circle}
is applicable and returns a \TYP{Circle}, but the second, which runs for such an
argument, returns only a \TYP{Round}, and it has no other instance.
The pair is allowed when the second declaration is itself generic:
%ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T = x
%ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T = x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Round}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)
\end{Fortress}
Its instance at any type to which it is applicable returns that type.
\revision{revival-overloading}{This section is new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 required overloaded declarations to have
identical static parameters and ignored them.
The rules stated are those of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn,
Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple
Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011),
which the compiled type checker applies, with its Return Type Rule checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; the pair refused above has the
shape of that paper's own example, which the compiled path used to accept and
then fail to verify.
The interpreter runs the pair allowed above, reading two declarations with
static parameters on their declared domains, each over its own instances, where
no pair of their parameter types excludes each other; the compiled code
generator fails on it (row~537 of the revival's gap ledger).
The compiled implementation adds one restriction that is not a rule of the
language.
When one declaration with static parameters is more specific than another that
declares as many static parameters of its own, the two must declare them of the
same kinds, position by position, and the return type of the more specific one
must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are identified
position by position; for its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration the call dispatches to (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger).
So it refuses this override, whose return type names its static parameters in
the other order, where \TYP{Pr} is an object with two type parameters:
%trait Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\A, B\]
%end
%object M extends Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\B, A\] = Pr[\B, A\](1)
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Maker}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{make}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket()\COLON \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object} M \KWD{extends} \TYP{Maker}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{make}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket()\COLON \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}B, A\rrbracket = \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}B, A\rrbracket(1)\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
The type group's paper of 2019 (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019)
instantiates a dispatched declaration from the dynamic types of the arguments
and the static type of the call, renaming static parameters freely
(\secref{resolving-overloading}); under it the override is valid, and the
restriction goes when the compiled dispatcher instantiates a declaration that
way.}

## Findings: departures with no row and no decision

Each is by reading; none was run. Each gives the rule, the code, what follows, and what would settle it.

1. **The exclusion test reads every static parameter as invariant.**
   - *Rule.* Constructability of a common subtype (`appendix.tex:203-206`): at a covariant parameter two instances cannot have one only where their arguments exclude; at a contravariant one, never. [Anc-Same-Trait] (`lang.tex:393-397`) admits two instances of a covariant trait where a third below both is an ancestor too.
   - *Code.* `checkP` (`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:541-555`) excludes wherever an argument pair is not equivalent (`:547-551`), while the subtype test reads the declared variance (`:274-280`).
   - *What follows*, only under `covariant` or `contravariant` (P-62's future work; row 404 holds the run-time half): under `trait C[\covariant S\]` with `trait Dog extends Animal` and `trait Cat extends Animal`, neither excluding the other, the hierarchy check refuses `object D extends { C[\Dog\], C[\Animal\] }`, which the rule admits; and the overloading check accepts `f(x: C[\Dog\])` beside `f(x: C[\Cat\])` as excluding, though `object DC extends C[\DogCat\]`, with `trait DogCat extends { Dog, Cat }`, is below both, so `f(DC)` has no most specific declaration. Nothing on microGPT's path uses variance.
   - *Settles it.* A note on row 404, or a row of its own, for worklist item 12: "the compiled checker's exclusion test reads every static parameter as invariant, so under `trait C[\covariant S\]` it counts `C[\Dog\]` and `C[\Cat\]` as excluding and refuses an object that extends `C[\Dog\]` and `C[\Animal\]`".
2. **The compiled dispatch matches an arrow-typed parameter without contravariance.**
   - *Rule.* [M-Arrow-Arrow] flips the variance in the domain (`appendix.tex:298-301`), as [Sub-Arrow] does (`:65-67`).
   - *Code.* `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/repository/ProjectProperties.java:327-328`), so the dispatcher's type structures get no contravariant variance (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1188`); the branch that would infer through a contravariant occurrence stops the code generator (`:1708-1709`).
   - *What follows.* A compiled call with function arguments can pick another declaration than walk; the record knows the switch (`explorations/coordinator/map/dormant-code.md:186`, the team's `c35aac139` of 2012; `fortress-repo` skill, `compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path"), but no ledger row holds it and no decision says whether phase 5's dispatcher turns it on.
   - *Settles it.* A row in the ledger's section on overloading on the compiled path, and a probe of a pair over `(Shape -> ZZ32)` and `(Circle -> ZZ32)` on both paths.
3. **The distinctness premises were not found.**
   - *Rule.* `distinct(x̄)` in [D-Method] and [T-Closure] (`lang.tex:211`; `resolve.tex:10`), `distinct(P̄)` in [D-Trait] and [D-Object] (`lang.tex:168`, `:187`), `distinct(P̄, Q̄)` in [D-Method] (`lang.tex:215`).
   - *Code.* The disambiguator gathers parameter names into a `Set[Id]` (`scala_src/disambiguator/ExprDisambiguator.scala:837-841`), whose equality compares spans (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes/Id.java:54-72`), and its loop for two equal names in one binding group (`ExprDisambiguator.scala:766-783`) compares elements that the set already holds as distinct, within bounds (`0 until vars.size - 2`, `:776-777`) that never reach the last element. No other check was found for parameter names or static parameter names.
   - *What follows.* Not established: another phase may refuse `f(x: ZZ32, x: ZZ32)` or `g[\T, T\](x: T)`.
   - *Settles it.* One probe of each on both paths; then a row if either loads.
4. **The specificity test can hold by a `Bottom` instance.**
   - *Rule.* [E-Sub] and [U-Sub] put no `Bottom` in a parameter's place (`rules.tex:159`, `:171`); "our type system requires that both static and dynamic type inference algorithms instantiate type parameters with non-`Bottom` types" (`resolve.tex:239-241`).
   - *Code.* `subEDsolution` solves the other domain's parameters with `solve`, not `solveToBounds` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1068`; `scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:189-196`): a variable that no lower bound fixes takes the join of none (`scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala:597-599`), and one left open is set to `Bottom` (`STypesUtil.scala:2126-2129`); `subUA` likewise (`TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:141`).
   - *What follows.* Where `Bottom` is the only solution, the checker reads a pair as nested that the rule does not: with `object Red end` and `object Blue end`, `f(g: Blue -> ZZ32)` is more specific than `f[\T extends Red\](g: T -> ZZ32)` at `T = Bottom`. The paper's rule reads them as neither nested nor excluding. Whether any pair of the one library turns on it is unmeasured.
   - *Settles it.* A probe of that pair; a `Bottom`-free solve in `subEDsolution` if it is accepted.
5. **A static parameter's bound may name a parameter declared after it.**
   - *Rule.* Restriction (1) of [Binding-Step] (`lang.tex:407-411`, `:438-439`).
   - *Code.* The checker binds a declaration's static parameters together (`scala_src/typechecker/staticenv/KindEnv.scala:40-51`); only the code generator refuses a bare-variable bound that names a later parameter (`OverloadSet.java:1501-1515`).
   - *What follows.* No consequence is established: the compiled dispatcher's right-to-left pass is the dual of the paper's (§4), and the paper's restriction (2), which the library breaks, is question 4.
   - *Settles it.* Phase 5's dispatcher design, which must fix one orientation.

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, as P-44 does for the closure of `AnyIntegral`, by one rule that peer languages share. F-225 states the rule as built.
